explanation:
[FEATURE: hr]
[EFFECT] Demand follows a strong double-peak pattern across the day. Contributions are most negative in the very early morning (around 4 a.m., SHAP ≈ −3.5), meaning very few rentals are predicted then. They rise sharply to a morning-rush peak around 8 a.m. (~+0.9), dip slightly mid-morning, climb again to the highest point of the day around 5 p.m. (~+1.0), and then fall steadily back through the evening.
[IMPORTANCE] This is by far the single most important feature (importance 0.833), dwarfing all others; the hour of day alone drives the largest swings in predicted demand.

[FEATURE: temp]
[EFFECT] The effect is non-monotonic: very cold temperatures (normalised value near 0, i.e. around 0 °C) strongly suppress demand (SHAP ≈ −0.9), contributions rise steeply through mild conditions, and peak at a normalised temperature of roughly 0.65–0.75 (about 27–31 °C). Beyond that, very high temperatures cause the contribution to fall back, so extreme heat also reduces predicted demand.
[IMPORTANCE] Third most important feature (importance 0.197), essentially tied with year; temperature has a large effect spanning nearly 1.1 log-units from coldest to peak.

[FEATURE: yr]
[EFFECT] This feature acts as a simple step: hours in 2011 (value 0) consistently receive a negative contribution (roughly −0.25 to −0.35), while hours in 2012 (value 1) receive a positive contribution (roughly +0.15 to +0.25), reflecting that the bike-share system grew substantially between the two years.
[IMPORTANCE] Second most important feature (importance 0.200), with a clear and consistent shift of about 0.5 log-units between the two years.

[FEATURE: mnth]
[EFFECT] Contributions are most negative in January (down to about −0.7), rise progressively through spring, and remain broadly positive from May through November (around +0.1 to +0.25). December dips back toward −0.4, so winter months at both ends of the year suppress predicted demand while the warmer mid-year months support it.
[IMPORTANCE] Fifth most important feature (importance 0.118); its effect is meaningful but roughly half the size of temperature or year.

[FEATURE: hum]
[EFFECT] The effect is non-monotonic, with penalties at both extremes. Very low humidity (near 0 %) pulls contributions down to about −0.5; moderate humidity (roughly 20–60 %) keeps contributions near zero or slightly positive; and very high humidity (above about 80 %) causes contributions to plunge sharply, reaching as low as −0.8 near full saturation.
[IMPORTANCE] Sixth most important feature (importance 0.077); a moderate influence, primarily visible as a strong negative drag under very humid conditions.

[FEATURE: weathersit]
[EFFECT] Each weather category produces a distinct step down in contribution: clear sky (1) gives a small positive boost (~+0.04), mist or cloud (2) is approximately neutral to slightly negative (~0 to −0.05), and light rain or snow (3) causes a large negative pull (SHAP ranging from about −0.15 to −0.6). The rare heavy-rain category (4) sits in a moderately negative range based on very few data points.
[IMPORTANCE] Seventh most important feature (importance 0.051); a noticeable but secondary influence, mainly felt when conditions deteriorate to light precipitation or worse.

[FEATURE: weekday]
[EFFECT] Each day of the week shows a wide spread of contributions (driven by interactions with hour), but the cloud centres tell the main story: mid-week days (Monday–Friday) tend to sit around +0.1 to +0.2, while Sunday and Saturday centres are closer to zero and include the largest downward tails (reaching about −0.9 on Sundays). On average, weekdays add slightly more to predicted demand than weekend days.
[IMPORTANCE] Fourth most important feature (importance 0.173); a meaningful driver, especially when combined with the hour-of-day effect.

[FEATURE: windspeed]
[EFFECT] The trend is broadly downward: at very low wind speeds contributions hover near zero, and as wind speed increases the effect becomes progressively more negative, reaching around −0.2 to −0.4 at moderate speeds and approaching −0.7 at the highest observed speeds. Higher wind consistently reduces predicted demand.
[IMPORTANCE] Eighth most important feature (importance 0.020); a minor but directionally clear negative effect, notably smaller than all other features.

[FEATURE: holiday]
[EFFECT] Non-holiday hours (value 0) cluster almost exactly at zero — the model sees no effect. Holiday hours (value 1) show a wide spread of contributions (roughly −1.2 to +0.5), with the centre of the cloud sitting around −0.2 to −0.3, indicating a slight average reduction in predicted demand on public holidays, though individual hours vary considerably.
[IMPORTANCE] Least important feature in the model (importance 0.012); its effect is largely negligible and highly variable.

[RECOMMENDATION] Staffing and bike-redistribution plans should be built primarily around the hour of the day — particularly the sharp morning (≈8 a.m.) and evening (≈5 p.m.) peaks — and adjusted for temperature, since warm mild days can roughly double predicted rentals compared with cold or very hot ones. All other factors, including weather and weekday type, provide useful fine-tuning but are secondary to getting the time-of-day and temperature conditions right.
